en: The Sūtra on the Original Vows and Deeds of the Bodhisattva, in one fascicle, translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling at the site of enlightenment in Magadha; having first attained Buddhahood, his radiance...

The light was exceedingly bright, and there naturally appeared precious lotus lion-thrones; such were the seats upon which all Buddhas of antiquity sat. Their moral virtue, dignified demeanor, and marks of excellence were identical; their bodies and minds were pure, and their meritorious deeds were universally perfected. They clearly and thoroughly illumined the realms of people, lands, and dharmas; regarding the past, future, and present, they were free from all obstructions. Having arisen in the world, they were entirely equal in every respect.

At that time, the bodhisattvas assembled there were all in their final birth before Buddhahood; they had attained mastery of spiritual powers and reached subtle perfection, traveling throughout the ten directions to guide and benefit sentient beings. They opened the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, revealed the essentials of *nirvāṇa*, and fully entered into the faculties of others. Possessing the merit of knowledge of past lives and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they transformed and instructed through gradual stages. Understanding both internal and external phenomena, they remained unshakable from beginning to end. Their realization was equal to that of all buddha-lands, free from discrimination. They extolled the names of the Buddhas beyond measure, and regarding the affairs of the three miserable realms, there was nothing they did not penetrate. At last, they all sighed in praise, saying:

“The Buddha has thought of us and established our great resolve, enabling us to fully perceive all the excellences and defects within the various Buddha-worlds, the most sublime lands where Buddhas dwell and reside, the flourishing propagation of their teachings, their radiant supernormal powers, their instruction of devas and humans, and their revelation of the meaning of the Dharma. We have come to know the fundamental activities of the Buddhas—the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmana*), the ten treasuries (*kośa*), the ten vows (*praṇidhāna*), the ten clarities (*vidyā*), the ten concentrations (*samādhi*), the ten manifestations (*abhinirhāra*), and the ten seals (*mudrā*). He has severed our blemishes as well as all doubts and delusions, manifesting for us entirely the Buddha’s conduct, wisdom, spiritual power, and strength, his meditative absorptions, his immeasurable transformations according to the occasion, his four ways of non-protection, his four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), his eighteen unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*), all his sagely insights, his unsurpassed virtue and path, and the full unfolding of all his manifold qualities.”
To the east, infinitely far away, lies the realm of Fragrant Forest;
the Buddha there is named Entering Diligence, and the Bodhisattva is named Reverent Head.
To the south, infinitely far away, lies the realm of Joyful Forest.
The Buddha’s name is Unforsaken Joy; the Bodhisattva’s name is Chief of Enlightenment.
To the west, beyond the infinite, lies the land of Flower Forest;
the Buddha’s name is Practicing Diligence; the Bodhisattva’s name is Chief of Jewels.
To the north, infinitely far away, lies the realm of Dōrin;
the Buddha there is named Gyōshōjin, and the Bodhisattva is called Eishu.
To the northeast, infinitely far away, lies the realm of Shōren.
The Buddha’s name is Compassionate Diligence; the Bodhisattva’s name is Virtue Chief.
To the southeast, at the limitlessness [of space], is the Golden Forest Land;
the Buddha’s name is Exhaustive Diligence; the Bodhisattva’s name is Eye Chief.
To the southwest, infinitely far away, lies the Jewel Forest Land;
the Buddha there is named Supreme Diligence, and the Bodhisattva is named Bright Head.
To the northwest, infinitely far away, lies the Vajra Land.
The Buddha’s name is Ekayāna-tāraka; the Bodhisattva’s name is Dharmottara.
In the infinite region below, there is a crystal realm where the Buddha’s name is Brahma-vīrya and the Bodhisattva’s name is Prajñottara.
In the infinite distance above, there is the world-system called Forest of Desire;
the Buddha there is named Supreme Diligence, and the Bodhisattva is named Worthy Head (Bhadramukha).

These Bodhisattvas, led by Worthy Head—who is foremost among them—each accompanied by countless superior beings, came and prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, then sat upon lotus flowers to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Reverent Head, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, exclaimed:
"How wonderful! This assembly of superior men is unprecedented;
observe their dwelling place, the purity of this Buddha-land, and how they are clothed in the Tathāgata’s virtuous precepts, practicing the subtle and wondrous to perfect the roots of enlightenment."
By the power of his strength, he expounds the sutras and the Dharma, having attained the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority.
According to whether the lands are pure or turbid, he delivers sentient beings without limit; he disperses the transformative influence of the Way so that it reaches everywhere.

Within this buddha-field, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of distinct nations, where the wise and the foolish, the beautiful and the ugly, the tall and the short, and those with long or short lifespans, all differ in their various languages.
All heard of the Buddha’s virtues and each named him according to their own understanding:
some named the Buddha the Great Sage; some named him the Great Śramaṇa; some called him the Benefactor of the Multitudes;
some called him the Divine Man; some termed him the Brave and Wise; some termed him the World-Honored One; some called him the Able Confucian; and some called him the Ascended Immortal. Or...

Some call him the Celestial Master, others call him the Most Victorious; thus, among the gods and people of the ten directions, there are countless hundreds of millions who invoke him by various names as Buddha.
All of these are disciples whom he has instructed through the proclamation of the Way and its transformation, ever since he first resolved to attain enlightenment.

At that time, the Buddha emitted light from the wheel-mark on the soles of his feet, which illuminated all the minor lands within the Buddha-field. A single minor land consists of one Mount Sumeru around which the sun and moon revolve, illuminating the four continents—Pūrvavideha in the east, Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north—as well as the great oceans surrounding them, the encircling Iron Walls, and the twenty-eight heavens above; such a realm constitutes one minor land, and throughout the ten directions, there are a total of ten billion of these.
At that time, there appeared ten billion Sumeru mountains, ten billion suns and moons, as well as the heavens of the Four Great Kings,
the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
the Brahmā Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, and the Parīttābha Heaven.
...the Heaven of Water-Travel, the Heaven of Subtle Water, the Heaven of Immeasurable Water, the Heaven of Water-Sound, the Heaven of Limited Purity,
the Heaven of Universal Purity, the Heaven of Luminous Purity, the Heaven of Guarding the Wondrous, the Heaven of Subtle Wonders, the Heaven of Vast Wonders,
the Heaven of Ultimate Wonders, the Heaven of Loved Merit, the Heaven of Supreme Love, the Heaven of the Near Limit, and the Heaven of Excellent Contemplation.
The Heaven of Gods, the Heaven of Swift Vision, the Heaven of Freedom from Ties and Affection, the Heaven of Wisdom of Consciousness, and the Heaven of Wisdom Beyond Conceptualization—
up to the twenty-eighth Heaven of Formlessness— each has ten billion [deities].
This is a single buddha-field called the Sahā World, wherein Śākyamuni Buddha has manifested ten billion transformation bodies that pervade it entirely.
At that time, devas and humans behold these many small lands, and the various buddhas and bodhisattvas appear as if they were close at hand.
Chapter Two: On Vows and Practices The Bodhisattva Jñānaśīra asked the Bodhisattva Gauravaśīra:

"By what original practice did you attain the holy path to Buddhahood, such that your body, speech, and mind are pure, you do not harbor thoughts of others' evils, and you cause the entire world to likewise [be so]?"

Having identified their shortcomings, his benevolence and compassion were exceedingly great; his inner nature was clear and lucid, far surpassing that of other disciples and those with individual enlightenment.
No demonic influences whatsoever could move or disturb him. He was born with an upright appearance and incomparable physical marks;
his lineage was noble and honorable, and he knew how to revere the Buddha-dharma. He maintained his resolve with great strength and constantly practiced the four [immeasurables].
They were of equal high talent and keen intelligence, diligent, courageous, and robust; they cultivated the roots of myriad virtues and the various *pāramitās*;
their deeds were immeasurable, and they were always born in lands of merit.

Their words and appearance were trusted, they subdued their minds and rectified their intentions, gathered their thoughts to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and understood the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as the four great elements.
Mastery of the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the twelve links of dependent origination; unhindered in the seven factors of enlightenment and penetrating the wisdom of the ten powers;
extensively entering all paths to rescue those in peril and resolve their distress; revered by Śakra and Brahmā;
dispelling the darkness like a lamp and illuminating the world like the sun and moon; ferrying multitudes like a boatman—his virtue surpasses that of the sages.
"As the foremost among those in the three realms, desiring to accomplish this path,
what should one practice? Guṇaśīrṣa replied,
"Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
One’s aspirations should look toward the lofty and far-reaching, reaching the utmost in great compassion and pitying all in the ten directions.

If sons or daughters of good family wish to attain the Way of the Buddha, they should first rectify their own bodies, ensuring that speech and thought correspond; they should orally practice the scriptures, mentally contemplate what can be enacted, reform the past, and cultivate the future, never relinquishing the intent for the Way. By accumulating merit and performing good deeds, bestowing kindness without weariness, then whatever one asks about shall be fully attainable.

One who is a bodhisattva must diligently receive and study [the teachings], following the Buddha’s instructions without adding or subtracting anything; they should bind themselves with vows, keep in mind the peace of the world, uphold the precepts and cultivate aspirations, thereby establishing the foundation of virtue.
While observing the precepts at home, one should wish that all beings may resolve their greedy desires and enter into the dharma of emptiness.
While serving one’s parents with filial piety, one should wish that all beings may provide universal protection and care, enabling them to attain the Way of the Buddha.
When obeying the instructions of one's wife and children, one should wish that all sentient beings escape the prison of craving and have no heart of longing or attachment.
When obtaining the five desires, one should wish that all sentient beings enter into purity,
their minds free from any clinging.
When among music and entertainment, may all beings attain the joy of the Dharma and the patience of gladness.
When wearing precious necklaces and ornaments, may all beings cast off their heavy burdens and be free from the desire for finery.
Upon seeing various court ladies, one should wish that all sentient beings cast off attachment to form and be free from lewd and licentious behavior.
When ascending a multi-storied pavilion, one should wish that all sentient beings ascend the Hall of Dharma and receive all the Buddha’s sutras.
While staying in a chamber, one should wish that all beings awaken to the foulness of the body and no longer seek sensual pleasure.
When giving away all possessions, one should wish that all beings cultivate merit to rescue others and never fall into stinginess or greed.
If one feels weary of and detests the household life, one should wish that all beings swiftly attain liberation, free from all constraints and attachments.
If one leaves the household life, one should wish that all beings depart from suffering, affliction, and transgression, attaining peace through the Right Path.
Entering a Buddhist temple, one should wish that all beings draw near to the Buddha and practice the Dharma,
free from further obstructions.
Visiting teachers and friends, one should wish that all beings attain enlightenment and enter the Way of Rightness, so that they may all fulfill their aspirations.
When requesting the relinquishing of transgressions, one should wish that all sentient beings achieve their resolve and study without mid-course regret.
When shedding the white robes of a layperson, one should wish that all sentient beings understand the Way and cultivate virtue without indolence.
Receiving and donning the kāṣāya, may all beings wear the dharma-robes in their conduct, their minds free from defilement.
Shaving off the beard and hair, may all beings cast aside all finery and adornments, free from all weariness.
Having become a śramaṇa, may all beings receive and practice the Buddha’s intent,
guiding and enlightening the world.
Having received the perfected precepts, may all beings attain the skillful means of the Way and the perfection of wisdom.
When guarding the prohibitions of the Path, one should wish that all beings uphold the laws and precepts, never transgressing the teachings of the Dharma.
When first receiving the Upādhyāya, one should wish that all beings may,
like the mind in dhyāna, contemplate liberation.
Receiving instruction from teachers, great and small, may all beings uphold the sacred teachings of the Buddha and never forget what they have received.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed aspiration.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all beings penetrate deeply into the treasury of the sutras,
their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all beings rely upon the assembly of noble ones and attain deliverance through the Right Path.
Whenever opening a door or gate, one should wish that all beings open and manifest the Dharma, reaching unto *nirvāṇa*.
When closing a door or gate, one should wish that all beings shut off the evil paths,
so that their transgressions may be completely eliminated.
Upon entering the room, one should wish: May all sentient beings be peaceful, tranquil, and serene, and attain the mind of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
When spreading the bedding, one should wish: May all sentient beings enter the path of the Mahāyāna and bring peace and security to the world.
When sitting in repose, one should wish that all sentient beings sit beneath the Bodhi tree,
their minds free from attachment. When entering a gathering,
one should wish that all sentient beings achieve morality, concentration, and wisdom, and attain liberation, deliverance, and insight.
While counting the breaths, one should wish that all sentient beings may leave their homes and be free from worldly thoughts.
While guarding the mind, one should wish that all sentient beings may not be negligent and remain free from distracting thoughts.
Realizing that consciousness is impermanent, arouse the mind of diligence; when descending from your seat, you should vow:
"May all sentient beings tread upon the tracks of the Buddha, their minds unshakable."
When putting on the lower garment, one should wish: May all sentient beings always know shame and remorse, restraining their thoughts and guarding the Way.
When tying the belt, one should wish: May all sentient beings fasten their belts to cultivate goodness, their resolve never slackening.
Next, putting on the inner robe, he should wish that all beings be respectful, reverent, and cautious, free from arrogance and indolence.
Donning the upper dharma-robe, he should wish that all beings wear the exemplary model of the sages and be diligent in the practice of the Path.
When attending to the calls of nature, may all beings eliminate defilements and be free from lust, anger, and ignorance.
After finishing and approaching water for purification, may all beings become gentle and flexible, pure and refined.
When the water is pure, may all sentient beings wash themselves with the Dharma,
so that they are no longer subject to evil dispositions.
When holding a willow branch in hand, may all sentient beings learn the words of the Dharma to brush away all defilements.
When rinsing the mouth and cleaning the teeth, one should wish that all sentient beings cleanse their natures and dispositions until they abide in purity.
When washing the hands, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain soft and pure palms to grasp and uphold the Way of the sutras.
When washing the face, one should wish: May all sentient beings always turn toward purity, their minds free from blemish.
When leaving the door, one should wish: May all sentient beings, as the Buddha desires, emerge and deliver others across the three realms.
When turning toward the Way, one should wish that all sentient beings turn toward the unsurpassed Way,
their resolve never regressing; when practicing the Way,
one should wish that all sentient beings roam within the boundless, never resting midway.
Ascending the slope, may all sentient beings aspire to joyfully ascend the supreme path, free from all doubt and difficulty.
Descending the slope, may all sentient beings aspire to enter deeply into the vast,
profound, and subtle Dharma.
When walking on a winding path, one should wish that all beings discard crooked and devious intentions and act without malice or resentment.
When walking on a straight path, one should wish that all beings attain a mind of impartial correctness and speak without flattery or deceit.
Seeing dust raised by the wind, one should wish that all beings clarify their studies and cultivate their conduct,
so that their minds are not distracted or disordered.
Seeing rain settling the dust, one should wish that all beings subdue their will through great compassion, so that no discursive thoughts arise.
When resting under a tree, one should wish that all beings subdue their minds within the Way and never grow weary of contemplating the meaning of the scriptures.
When entering a forest or marsh, one should wish that all beings study to become scholars of the Confucian tradition and nurture their disciples through virtue.
Aspiring to what is lofty and great, accumulating merit without satiety, and seeing thorns and brambles on the path,
one should wish that all sentient beings may have the three poisons extinguished and be free from any intent to harm.
Encountering a tree with fine leaves, one should wish that all sentient beings may shade themselves with the Way and enter the samādhis of dhyāna.
Encountering a tree with profuse and flourishing blossoms, one should wish that all sentient beings may be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and all the secondary characteristics.
Seeing fruits and melons in full abundance, one should wish that all beings initiate the practices of the Bodhi-tree and attain the unsurpassed fruit.
Seeing flowing streams, one should wish that all beings obtain the flow of the true channels and enter the ocean-like wisdom of the Buddha.
All merits and virtues are filled with the practice of wisdom;
if one sees a spring of water, one should wish that all sentient beings enter the profound ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, so that their inquiries are inexhaustible.
Gazing afar at rivers and seas, may all sentient beings enter the profound treasury of the Buddha and its inexhaustible Dharma.
Seeing people drawing water from a well, may all sentient beings open their hearts to receive the Dharma and attain the single flavor of the Way.
When crossing a bridge, one should wish that all beings build bridges of Dharma, ferrying people across without ceasing.
Seeing the cultivation of gardens and orchards, one should wish that all beings weed out defilements and evils,
so that the roots of desire do not arise.
Seeing fields of rice and grain, one should wish that all beings extensively plant roots of merit and virtue, remaining free from calamities and afflictions.
Seeing a beautiful garden or orchard, one should wish that all beings attain complete upholding and be fully endowed with the teachings of the Way.
Seeing a village or a house, one should wish that all beings always abide in benevolence and wisdom,
so that the Way remains free from peril.
Seeing a hall for refined study, one should wish that all beings lecture upon and recite the scriptures and the Way, progressing daily without decline.
Seeing a gathering of people, one should wish that all beings fulfill their merits and attain Buddhahood, forming a community of disciples.
Seeing someone living in seclusion, one should wish that all beings be tranquil and non-active,
dwelling their minds in the sacred scriptures.
Upon seeing a śramaṇa, may all beings be endowed with extensive learning and the precepts, teaching others without weariness.
Upon seeing a follower of a heterodox path, may all beings distance themselves from false views and enter the Eightfold Noble Path.
Upon seeing a seer, may all beings be fully endowed with mental conduct,
so that their desires are fulfilled.
Upon reaching a city or town, may all beings maintain the precepts in their entirety, so that their minds are free from deficiency.
Upon seeing a palace or imperial quarters, one should wish that all sentient beings possess clear intelligence that shines afar, and that all virtues be universally established.
If one sees a sovereign or emperor, one should wish that all sentient beings may receive and uphold the holy transformation,
in accordance with the teachings of the True Path.
Upon seeing a prince, one should wish that all beings tread the path of the Buddha’s sons and be born through transformation within the Dharma.
If one sees high officials, one should wish that all beings be clear in their understanding of principle and assist in benefiting the world.
Seeing various ministers and officials, one should wish that all beings be loyal, upright, compliant, and virtuous,
free from any stubborn or predatory intent. Seeing those clad in armor,
one should wish that all beings vow to don the armor of the Dharma, never deviating from their original vows.
Seeing those who are dull-witted, one should wish that all beings be courageous in the way of righteousness and achieve the four fearlessnesses.
Seeing those who are sorrowful, one should wish that all beings be free from all terrors and never again experience grief or distress.
Seeing those who laugh and rejoice, one should wish that all beings abandon the fleeting pleasures that amuse them with the five desires.
Seeing those who undergo toil and suffering, one should wish that all beings attain the path of Nirvana and be delivered from all calamities.
Seeing those who are at ease and happy, one should wish that all beings may be as peaceful and joyful as the Buddha,
serene and free from affliction.
Seeing those who are sick and ill, one should wish that all beings may realize that emptiness is not the body, and thus be free from the thought of suffering and pain.
May all sentient beings attain the adamantine form, free from decay or diminution.
When seeing those who are ugly or deformed, may all sentient beings abandon foul and evil conduct,
adorning themselves with virtue.
Seeing a person of upright appearance, one should wish that all beings have sincere and straightforward conduct and cherish the Dharma.
Seeing a person who repays kindness, one should wish that all beings mindfully reflect upon the Buddha’s benevolence and virtue, and practice the deeds of a Bodhisattva.
Seeing those who are ungrateful, one should wish that all beings subdue their minds and humble their wills,
casting away all evils.
Seeing those who are greedy, one should wish that all beings practice the gift of Dharma throughout the world, free from the mind of stinginess and greed.
Carrying the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), one should wish that all beings rely upon the Dharma and spread its transformative influence.
Carrying the alms bowl (*pātra*), one should wish that all beings receive offerings with awareness and cultivate the six dharmas of respect.
Entering a village for alms, may all beings seek according to the Dharma of the precepts, free from doubt or delusion.
Upon reaching the gates of others' homes, may all beings enter the gate of *dhāraṇī* and perceive all dharmas.
Upon entering a person’s hall or chamber, one should wish that all beings ascend the sacred hall of the Buddha and practice the profound and subtle.
When people do not give food, one should wish that all beings attain the wisdom of Prajñā, being without expectation and without attachment.
When the host has not yet prepared the meal, one should wish that all beings leave the three evil realms behind and be free from thoughts of hunger and thirst.
When receiving the empty alms bowl, one should wish that all beings attain the nature of emptiness and desirelessness.
When receiving a full alms-bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings may fully accomplish the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment.
When holding the bowl with rice, one should wish that all sentient beings may make offerings of the Dharma, their resolve set upon the Great Way.
When sitting with an honest person, one should wish that all beings be pure and modest,
knowing shame so that their actions are never false.
When sitting with a greedy person, one should wish that all beings have no forced countenance or base, covetous hearts.
When obtaining fragrant and delicious food, one should wish that all sentient beings know moderation and have few desires, their minds free from attachment.
When obtaining unwholesome food, one should wish that all sentient beings realize the body is an illusory phenomenon,
for which the pleasant and the unpleasant are no different.
Raising the rice toward the mouth, one should wish that all sentient beings may fully obtain all sutras and the flavor of the Buddhas' Dharma.
While eating various flavors, one should wish that all sentient beings may find every taste to be like that of the Buddha, transformed into nectar.
When the meal is finished, may all sentient beings be filled with virtuous conduct and attain the ten powers.
When expounding the sutras and preaching the Dharma, may all sentient beings have their minds opened and enlightened, awakening immediately upon hearing the Dharma.
When pronouncing the blessing for the alms-offering, one should pray: "May all sentient beings attain thorough mastery of the twelve divisions of the Buddha’s scriptures.
When rising from their seats and departing, one should pray: "May all sentient beings reach ultimate perfection and obtain the three kinds of ambrosia."
If one wishes to enter the water, may all sentient beings purify their body, speech, and mind, becoming equal to those in the three miserable realms.
When bathing the body, may all sentient beings wash away the defilements of the mind and perceive the limit of birth and death.
When the midsummer heat is extreme, may all sentient beings attain the samādhi of coolness and extinguish all suffering.
When the freezing cold is intense, may all sentient beings have their hearts cooled so that craving is eliminated, and they are no longer subject to worldly desires.
When reciting the sutras and verses, one should wish that all beings may have a broad understanding of all dharmas and never again forget them.
If one should behold a Buddha, one should wish that all beings may always meet with Buddhas and practice the seven factors of enlightenment.
Upon seeing an image of the Buddha, one should wish that all sentient beings behold the ten directions with eyes free from obstruction.
When prostrating before the Buddha, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the Way as the Buddha has, such that no one can see the crown of their heads.
Bowing one's head and rising, one should wish that all sentient beings may, like the Buddha’s intention, be noble and unsurpassed.
When first about to circumambulate the stupa, one should wish that all sentient beings practice and bestow blessings and protection, fully realizing the intent of the Way.
Circumambulating the stupa three times, one should wish that all sentient beings attain a single-minded resolve and never sever the four joys.
While chanting and reciting the sutras, one should wish that all sentient beings mindfully contemplate the Buddha’s benevolence and virtue,
and practice the offering of the Dharma.
Having finished praising the Buddha, one should wish that all sentient beings possess the divine power and virtue of radiance, equal to the Dharma-body of the Buddha.
When about to wash one's feet at dusk, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) and pervade the ten directions.
When sleeping and resting in the dark of night, one should wish that all sentient beings leave behind the darkness and are no longer burdened by the five hindrances.
When waking from sleep, one should wish that all sentient beings may attain the eighteen unexcelled qualities of a Buddha.
This is the Bodhisattva who practices both precepts and vows, who loves universally and bestows extensively, never abandoning the ten directions.

Chapter Three: The Ten Stages (Daśabhūmi). At that time, in this Sahā world, the Indras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven from ten billion worlds all, within the purple-blue palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, manifested lion thrones made of the seven treasures. They spread canopies of interlaced jewels and covered them with variegated silk rugs; having done so, they each bowed their heads and entreated the Buddha.

The Buddha, knowing all this in his mind, immediately manifested transformation bodies that pervaded all the palaces of the Śākyas. Each of these Buddhas was accompanied by a multitude of bodhisattvas, so that none among the celestial emperors failed to rejoice.
Furthermore, in each of the ten billion small kingdoms below, people continued to see the Buddha as before, without any diminution.

At that time, from the lands of the ten directions, there gathered once more the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, the Bodhisattva Śīlamati, the Bodhisattva Kalyāṇamati, the Bodhisattva Vīramati, the Bodhisattvas Cintāmati, Jñānamati, Nirūpaṇamati, Ekāgramati, Gauravamati, and Kṣayamati. Each came from the ten directions together with countless superior beings; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat upon lotus seats to one side.

The Bodhisattva Dharmamati, assuming a form exactly like that [of the Buddha], sat upright and concentrated his mind, entering the samādhi of "Beholding the Immeasurable Assemblies. He saw all the countless Buddhas of the ten directions, each extending their right hand to stroke his head, and they all said:
"Excellent!"
Dharmamati!

The Bodhisattva is courageous and steadfast, having attained this samādhi. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as well as Śākyamuni Buddha, have all already paid homage to you for establishing these merits. You cultivate subtle and wondrous eloquence, know the practice of emptiness and non-attachment, thoroughly expound the essentials of the Dharma, master the speech of all Buddhas, and understand the intentions of sentient beings.

"Your practice is already complete; you shall attain Buddhahood before long. I now command you to expound the ten stages of the bodhisattva, so that all students may universally know what is to be practiced.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, having attained the eloquence of a Buddha—possessing wisdom as clear and true as the ultimate reality, neither forgetting nor faltering—arose from his meditative concentration and said:
"O sons of noble family!..."

Those who seek Buddhahood have ten stages of dwelling; from antiquity to the present, all have attained accomplishment through these. Praised by the World-Honored Ones, they are in accord with the immeasurable; I shall now set them forth and explain them in detail, just as the Buddha has spoken.

What are the ten? First, the initial aspiration; second, the stage of purification; third, the stage of practice; fourth, the stage of noble birth; fifth, the stage of cultivation and completion; sixth, the stage of ascent through practice; seventh, the stage of non-retrogression; eighth, the stage of youthful truth; ninth, the stage of understanding birth; and tenth, the stage of the position of succession.

"What is meant by 'arousing the aspiration' (bodhicitta)? When a Bodhisattva abides in the Dharma, there are ten matters; that is to say, upon first seeing the Buddha, ten merits arise: first, seeing the Buddha’s physical excellence; second, his body being complete with the marks and signs;

third, the manifestation of supernatural transformations through psychic power; fourth, the profundity of his Way and virtue; fifth, the incomparability of his dignified demeanor and methods; sixth, his knowledge of the intentions of others’ minds; seventh, the clarity of the sutras and teachings he expounds; eighth, the truth and understanding of what he says; ninth, seeing the suffering of birth and death; and tenth, taking pleasure in the essence of the Buddha-Dharma. Through these, one gradually attains understanding and thus arouses the aspiration for the Way."

To fully comprehend the wisdom of the Buddha’s ten powers, there are ten trainings: one should know how to honor and serve all Buddhas; one should understand how to expound the virtues of Bodhisattvas;

one should clearly realize the root of birth and death; one should aspire to cultivate noble merit; one should cause one's conduct to transcend the three realms; one should study the meritorious deeds of all Buddhas; one should seek to behold all Buddhas again; one should practice and cultivate all profound samādhis; one should compassionately mind those who suffer from transgressions; and one should turn back from the wheel of birth and death. This is the stage of the initial resolve for the highest goal.
"What is meant by 'cultivating the ground' (bhūmi-karman)?
There are ten matters for the Bodhisattva’s abiding in the Dharma that are to be studied in succession:

first, to contemplate the goodness of others; second, to purify the mind; third, to soften the will; fourth, to settle the resolve; fifth, to practice constant giving; sixth, to exercise loving-kindness; seventh, to benefit all under heaven; eighth, to assist in impartiality; ninth, to regard others as oneself; and tenth, to respect others as one's teacher."
Furthermore, there are ten trainings: one should frequently recite the sutras;

one should distance oneself from one’s native land; one should draw near to an enlightened teacher; one should learn virtuous speech; one should know the proper timing; one should be diligent; one should enter the essential; one should understand practice; one should not forget; and one should settle the mind. These constitute the successive practices for cultivating the ground.
"What is meant by 'that which should be practiced'?
There are ten matters regarding the Bodhisattva’s abiding in the Dharma, as set forth in the Sūtra:

first, seeing impermanence; second, seeing the suffering of birth; third, seeing the emptiness of conditioned formations; fourth, seeing that there is no self; fifth, seeing that there is no master; sixth, being without greed; seventh, being without attachment; eighth, being unconditioned; ninth, being without desire; and tenth, being without seeking."
Furthermore, there are ten trainings:

one should be mindful of persons, one should be mindful of lands, one should be mindful of the Dharma, one should be mindful of the earth element, one should be mindful of the water element, one should be mindful of the fire element, one should be mindful of the wind element, one should be mindful of the desire realm, one should be mindful of the form realm, and one should be mindful of the formless realm; with a mind free from attachment or longing, this is the differentiation of the stages of practice to be undertaken.
"What is meant by 'noble by birth'? There are ten matters in which a Bodhisattva abides in the Dharma, following the practice of the Buddha:

first, not returning to false paths; second, directing the mind single-mindedly toward the Buddha; third, contemplating the meaning of the Dharma; fourth, observing meritorious conduct; fifth, viewing people as like illusions; sixth, viewing lands as like dreams; seventh, viewing calamity and fortune as empty; eighth, viewing all dharmas as like phantoms; ninth, seeing no difference between suffering and pleasure; tenth, understanding the purity of Nirvana."
Furthermore, there are ten trainings:

one should know that one must contemplate that the mind of the Buddhas of the past is empty, the mind of the Buddhas of the future is empty, and the mind of the Buddhas of the present is empty; the Dharma of the Buddhas of the past is pure, the Dharma of the Buddhas of the future is pure, and the Dharma of the Buddhas of the present is pure; the Buddhas of the past are self-existent, the Buddhas of the future are self-existent, and the Buddhas of the present are self-existent. All Buddhas who arise are equal and without any difference; this is called the ground of noble birth through equanimity.
"What is meant by 'cultivation and accomplishment'?
There are ten matters in which a Bodhisattva abides in the Dharma to bring salvation to people:

first, providing skillful means for others; second, causing others to dwell in peace and security; third, providing relief and rescue for all people in the world; fourth, regarding all with loving-kindness; fifth, feeling compassion for sentient beings; sixth, causing others to rejoice; seventh, protecting and watching over people and things; eighth, exhorting them to follow the Path; ninth, manifesting purity for their sake; and tenth, enabling them to attain Nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, there are ten further trainings:

one should know that sentient beings have no essential core, no seed, no number, no creator, and no correctness; they are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and cannot be fully described; they are entirely empty—this is the ground for the cultivation and perfection of the noble practice.

"What is meant by 'ascending through practice'? There are ten matters in the Bodhisattva’s abiding in the Dharma, which, when fulfilled, lead to success: first, hearing praise of the Buddha or criticism of the Buddha, the mind remains unchanged;

second, hearing praise of the Dharma or disparagement of the Dharma, the mind remains unchanged; third, hearing of the virtues of Bodhisattvas or their faults, the mind remains unchanged; fourth, hearing people’s mutual evaluations, the mind remains unchanged; fifth, hearing that people are many or few, the mind remains unchanged; sixth, hearing that the sutras are numerous or few, the mind remains unchanged; seventh, hearing of the arising of suffering or the arising of joy, the mind remains unchanged; eighth, hearing that people are difficult to deliver or easy to deliver, the mind remains unchanged; ninth, hearing of the flourishing or the decline of the Dharma, the mind remains unchanged; tenth, encountering a time of the Way or a time without the Way, the mind remains unchanged."

Furthermore, there are ten trainings: the mind is without conceptualization; one does not accept conceptualization; one does not reckon a body; there is no "mine"; there is no view; there is no master; there is no recipient; one is like a magical transformation; one is unconditioned; and there is nothing whatsoever. These constitute the ground for ascending through the practice of exhaustive faith.
"What is meant by 'non-retrogression'? There are ten matters in which the Bodhisattva abides in the Dharma, his resolve being firm and strong:

first, non-retrogression whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha; second, non-retrogression whether there is the Dharma or no Dharma; third, non-retrogression whether there are Bodhisattvas or no Bodhisattvas; fourth, non-retrogression whether there are those seeking Buddhahood or none seeking Buddhahood; fifth, non-retrogression whether there is the attainment of Buddhahood or the non-attainment of Buddhahood; sixth, non-retrogression whether the noble path existed in the past or did not exist; seventh, non-retrogression whether the noble path exists now or does not exist; eighth, non-retrogression whether the noble path will exist in the future or will not exist; ninth, non-retrogression whether the three miserable realms are identical to the three realms or different from them; tenth, non-retrogression whether the Buddha’s wisdom is finite or infinite."

Furthermore, there are ten trainings: opening subtle wisdom to enter great wisdom; opening great wisdom to enter subtle wisdom; manifesting a single dharma to enter the myriad scriptures; manifesting the myriad scriptures to enter a single dharma; understanding sentient beings to enter the essential of emptiness; understanding the essential of emptiness to enter sentient beings; explaining conceptual thought to enter tranquil concentration; explaining tranquil concentration to enter conceptual thought; explaining limited purity to enter expansive thought; and explaining expansive thought to enter limited purity. These constitute the stage of progressive advancement without regression.
"What is meant by 'youthful truth' (kumārabhūta)? There are ten matters regarding the Bodhisattva’s abiding in the Dharma that follow wherever he enters:

first, no transgression of body, speech, or mind; second, being entirely without blemish; third, having a single-minded resolve toward whatever is born; fourth, seeing people and knowing their inner compassion; fifth, knowing what the minds of others believe; sixth, knowing what the intentions of others understand; seventh, not receiving the various conceptualizations of others; eighth, knowing the formation and destruction of all lands; ninth, swiftly reaching everywhere in the ten directions through spiritual power; and tenth, fully upholding all dharmas."

Furthermore, there are ten matters: learning to know the Buddha-worlds; learning the wisdom and capabilities of a Buddha; learning to manifest the miraculous powers of a Buddha; learning to adorn all Buddha-fields; learning to travel extensively through all lands; learning to answer the questions of the multitude through the Dharma; learning to manifest transformations that appear everywhere; learning for the Buddha’s voice to bring forth all dharmas; learning to turn the wheel [of the Dharma] throughout the ten directions; and learning to see countless Buddhas in a single thought-moment. These constitute the stage of the Pure Youth (Śuddhāvāsa-kumārabhūta).
"What is meant by 'comprehending birth'? There are ten matters of the Bodhisattva’s abiding in the Dharma through which one receives the vision of wisdom:

first, knowing in which realm all beings are born; second, knowing the fetters practiced by sentient beings; third, knowing the origins from which people have previously come; fourth, knowing the retributions of calamity and fortune resulting from the deeds people perform; fifth, knowing what dharmas people receive and practice; sixth, knowing the inclinations toward good or evil into which people's minds enter; seventh, knowing the various transformations of people's thoughts and intentions; eighth, knowing the purity or turbidity of the lands in the ten directions; ninth, knowing the immeasurable wisdom regarding the three miserable realms; and tenth, knowing how to explain the essential truths according to what is appropriate."

Furthermore, there are ten matters: learning the correct conduct of the Dharma King; learning the etiquette of the Dharma King; learning the establishment of the Dharma King; learning the coming and going of the Dharma King; learning the movements of the Dharma King; learning the majestic authority of the Dharma King; learning the sitting and rising of the Dharma King; learning the commands of the Dharma King; learning how the Dharma King pays homage to others; and learning how the Dharma King tours through the buddha-fields. These constitute the ground for receiving the prediction of enlightenment and the completion of birth.
"What is meant by 'the stage of succession' (kṣānti)? There are ten matters in which the Bodhisattva abides in the Dharma, such that wisdom finds it difficult to reach them:

first, one should contemplate and move countless lands; second, one should manifest illumination for countless lands; third, one should establish the Dharma for countless lands; fourth, one should open the way for the deliverance of countless lands; fifth, one should benefit and bring peace to countless lands; sixth, one should proclaim and awaken countless people; seventh, one should observe and know the intentions of sentient beings; eighth, one should know the infinite thoughts of sentient beings; ninth, one should cause countless people to enter the Dharma; tenth, one should manifest the clear understanding of human wisdom in successive order."
There are ten things that those born [in this world] cannot equal those in the stage of the successor (upapadya-bhūmi):

they cannot know the successor’s physical activities and mental conduct; his supernormal powers, meditative concentration, and mindfulness; his mastery of the past and knowledge of the present; his vision of future states of existence; his cultivation of the methods for purifying buddha-fields; the matters concerning the intentions of the sages; and the aspirations of the successor.

Furthermore, there are ten matters: to study the Buddha’s wisdom regarding the boundless three realms of suffering; to study the fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas; to study the dharma that is unattached to any phenomena; to study the bottomless treasury of all Buddhas; to study the divine wisdom that establishes their lands; to study the radiance that illuminates the ten directions; to study the meditative concentrations of the Buddha that move all realms; to study the skillful means that transform beings according to their inclinations; to study the universal teaching that brings all to accomplishment; and to study the assembly for the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

The reason for studying is the desire to know all things and to become universally proficient so that there is nothing further to learn; this is called being in the stage of "one who is next to Buddhahood" (Ekajātipratibaddha).

By accomplishing the ten sets of ten dharmas, one attains in the present life the succession to the unsurpassed, right, and true path, becoming a Most Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksambuddha) to deliver and liberate all under heaven.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Dharmamati Bodhisattva may truly be called a son of the Buddha.”

All Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions arise from this; this Dharma is boundless, its illumination is immeasurable, its deliverance of beings is infinite, and its wisdom-mind is inexhaustible.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, everyone was filled with great joy and paid homage to the Buddha.
This concludes the *Sūtra on the Original Vows and Deeds of the Bodhisattvas* spoken by the Buddha.
